title: 4: Categorical data basics
text:
What is categorical data?

Samples can take on one of several discrete values or groups

Nominal: no particular order to the groups
Ordinal: groups relate to each other in a specific order

Categories can be represented as strings or numeric types

Domain knowledge is necessary!




Let’s take a few minutes to brainstorm some examples

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Machine learning

To appropriately process the data, we need to know why we are doing it and what assumptions we’re making
Modern machine learning toolkits (such as scikit-learn) are so easy to use, they’re easy to use inappropriately
Goal: just enough understanding to use basic models responsibly

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Why are we processing data?



No reinforcement learning in this course, sorry

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
A selection of common models


Supervised

Linear/logistic regression
Decision trees
Support vector machines


Unsupervised

K-means clustering
Principle component analysis

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
No free lunch

A theory-heavy paper in 1996 showed that there is no one machine learning algorithm that excels in all situations
Subsequent work has confirmed this, e.g. a 2018 analysis
Tree-based methods, particularly gradient boosted trees tend to outperform other algorithms the most, but still have limitations
What does it mean to “outperform”?


Further reading: https://feat.engineering/01-introduction.html#sec-no-free-lunch

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Model evaluation: Classification

True positive: predicted positive, label was positive (\(TP\)) ✔️
True negative: predicted negative, label was negative (\(TN\)) ✔️
False positive: predicted positive, label was negative (\(FP\)) ❌ (type I)
False negative: predicted negative, label was positive (\(FN\)) ❌ (type II)
Accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions, given as:
\[\mathrm{accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}\]

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Precision and recall

Precision: Out of all the positive predictions, how many were correct? \[\mathrm{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\]
Recall: Out of all the positive labels, how many were correct? \[\mathrm{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\]
Specificity: Out of all the negative labels, how many were correct? \[\mathrm{specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}\]

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Confusion matrix

The axes might be reversed, but a good predictor will have strong diagonals
There’s also the F1 score, or harmonic mean of precision and recall: \[F1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\mathrm{precision} \cdot \mathrm{recall}}{\mathrm{precision} + \mathrm{recall}}\]
Better for unbalanced datasets, but still does not capture specificity


Check out the Wikipedia page for more ways of describing the same information

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
ROC Curves

The receiver operating characteristic curve is a plot of the true positive rate (recall or sensitivity) vs. false positive rate (1 - specificity) as the detection threshold changes
The diagonal is the same as random guessing
A perfect classifier would hug the top left corner



Fun fact: the name comes from WWII radar operators, where true positives were airplanes and false positives were noise

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Model evaluation: regression

For a predicted \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) and actual \(\mathbf{y}\), metrics include:

Mean squared error: \(MSE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\)
Root mean squared error: \(RMSE = \sqrt{MSE}\)
Mean absolute error: \(MAE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i - \hat{y}_i|\)
Mean absolute percentage error: \(MAPE = \frac{100}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left|\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{y_i}\right|\)
Coefficient of determination: \(R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2}\) (\(R^2\) has some caveats)

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Regression: ordinary least squares


In 1D, estimate modeled as: \(\hat{y_i} = wx_i + b\), where \(i\) denotes a sample
Vector form: \(\mathbf{\hat{y}} = w\mathbf{x} + b\)
Goal is to minimize the Mean Square Error:
\[\begin{aligned}
MSE &= \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m (\hat{y} - y_i)^2 = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m (b + w x_i - y_i)^2\\
MSE &= \frac{1}{m} (\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})^T (\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}\]

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Regression: N-dimensional

Most of the time we have \(N > 1\) features
N-D: \(\hat{y_i} = w_1x_{1i} + w_2x_{2i} + ... + w_nx_{ni} + b\)
Common to use a design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) to represent the feature values:
\[\mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1n} \\
1 & x_{21} & x_{22} & \cdots & x_{2n} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
1 & x_{m1} & x_{m2} & \cdots & x_{mn} \end{bmatrix}\]
where each row is an instance (sample) and each column is a feature.

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Regression: N-dimensional

We can rewrite the estimate in matrix notation: \[\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{\theta}\]
The MSE can be written as:
\[MSE = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2 = \frac{1}{m} (\mathbf{X} \mathbf{\theta} - \mathbf{y})^T (\mathbf{X} \mathbf{\theta} - \mathbf{y})\]
This has a closed form solution, but it is computationally expensive

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Comparison of supervised model families


Linear models


Very fast, particularly inference
Scalable to large number of features
Can model nonlinearity with kernel trick
Easy to regularize

 

Difficult to interpret
Sensitive to parameters and preprocessing
Data needs to be on same scale
Slow to train on large datasets



Decision Trees


Highly explainable
Fast to train
Few parameters to tune
Little preprocessing needed
Provides feature importance

 

Prone to overfitting
High variance
Poor extrapolation

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
Clustering: \(k\)-means


Goal: Partition \(N\) samples into \(k\) clusters
Naive algorithm:

Initialize \(k\) centroid locations
Assign each sample to the nearest centroid
Recalculate centroids for each cluster
Repeat steps 2-3 until clusters stabilize



\[\sum_{i=0}^N \min_{\mu_j \in C}(\Vert x_i - \mu_j \Vert^2)\]

title: 2. Basic machine learning models
text:
\(k\)-means pros and cons


Intuitive
Easy to implement
Relatively scalable (\(O(N)\))

 

Need to know how many clusters
Sensitive to initialization
Not guaranteed to converge to global minimum
Doesn’t like anisotropy and unequal variance



Scikit-learn has a great reference table of other clustering methods

title: 2: Basic Modelling
text:
Predicting Titanic survivorship
Consider this a “Hello, world!” of supervised learning! The Titanic survival dataset is one of the most popular practice datasets.

Open your copy of titanic.ipynb and run the first cell. Install any missing packages you encounter.
I’ve done some basic exploratory data analysis and constructed the pipeline for you, as we haven’t gotten to this in class yet. The pipeline is as follows:
pipeline = make_pipeline(
   make_column_transformer(
      (OneHotEncoder(), cat_feats),
      (StandardScaler(), num_feats)
   )
   # TODO: add some kind of classification model
)
Add a decision tree classifier to the pipeline.
Train and cross-validate your tree, choosing an appropriate scoring metric.






Tip



If your model complains about missing values (or some more obscure message about NaN), you might need to remove the Embarked feature — I missed that it actually has 2 missing features.


Experiment! Does your model seem like it’s working fairly well? If not, what could you change? Consider:

Dropping features that don’t add value
Training a forest of trees
Changing tree depth to avoid overfitting

As you make changes, record why you’re making the change and your observations. Since this may involve going back and tweaking just one or two lines of code, it’s okay to write these as comments in the code without copy/pasting the entire pipeline, e.g.:
# Started with max depth of 3 but it seemed like it wasn't learning enough
# Increasing to 4 improves predictions without overfitting
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(maxDepth=4)
Repeat, but with some kind of linear classification model, such as LinearSVC or LogisticRegression. What changes?

title: Assignment 1: Simple Modelling
text:
Setup
You may work in groups up to 3. Please join a group on D2L, then pick one person to accept the assignment and create the GitHub repository with the dataset. Whoever does this becomes the group manager and can invite team members with their GitHub username.






TipIf you make a mistake with groups



Don’t worry, this is the first time for all of us using Classroom50, and the platform itself is brand new. Let me know if you accidentally created two groups, or joined the wrong one; I can modify groups on the backend.


In your repo, you may store as many python files, Jupyter notebooks, draft documents, etc. However, please create one coherent report named assignment1 that includes:

Your group members’ names
Some key figures and commentary on data exploration
Description of your data processing decisions
A summary of your experiments
Figures and discussion on your final models

Your report can be in Markdown or PDF format. In these instructions, I’ve indicated where you should write in your report in an annoying bold face.
I encourage you to talk things through as you try different things. If you talk with classmates from a different group, cite their contribution. Similarly, if you use a web resource, add a link in the code — this is both polite, and a good habit to develop.

title: Assignment 1: Simple Modelling
text:
The problem
You are working for the provincial government and are asked to help predict staffing budgets. Salaries are considered a known quantity, but benefits (cash and non-cash) appear to be more variable. To address this, you must build two models:

a regression model to predict the total cash and non-cash benefits per employee
a classification model to identify employees with less than $20,000 in benefits1

The benefits_train.csv file in your starter repo has been created from the Alberta Salary and severance disclosure table; I have reserved a separate test set and will release it for your testing pleasure after the assignment is complete.

Preliminary EDA and processing
Exploratory data analysis is an important step in data processing, but it is not the main focus of this assignment. You will need to do just enough to have an understanding of what the data looks like, such as:

What features are present
Are there any obvious relationships between features
How many unique values (categorical) or what are the distributions (numeric)

The results of your EDA will inform your processing pipeline, such as choosing a categorical encoding approach.
In your report, include a key figure or two from your EDA and briefly describe what you see.


Regression model
Using your choice of regression model from Scikit-learn, create and train a regression model to predict the total benefits (NonCashBenefits + CashBenefits) for each employee. You will need to create this total benefits column, or as a separate vector.






Tip



Don’t forget to remove or exclude the CashBenefits and NonCashBenefits fields of your training dataframe!



You will need to do some basic processing on the training data, but don’t feel the need to use all the features! In your report, briefly justify the following decisions:

Which features should be included?
How should categorical features be encoded?
How should numeric features be transformed?

I recommend creating a Scikit-learn Pipeline to be able to fit your processing parameters and model all in one go.
Validate your model using cross-validation. An easy way to do this is with sklearn.model_selection.cross_val_score. You will need to choose an appropriate metric and pass it as the scoring parameter; feel free to experiment with multiple. In your report, briefly justify why the metric chosen was appropriate.
Iterate! Based on the results of cross-validation, try to improve your model. You can tweak your processing parameters, model parameters, or even choose a different model. Briefly document your experiments in your report, making note of any changes that have impact. > Don’t spend too much time refining your model — the goal is to learn about the process and the factors that impact the results, not to produce the absolute best predictive model possible.
When you’re happy with the results, document your final pipeline in your report. This can just be a copy/paste of your pipeline construction code.

At this stage, you don’t have final test data, so the process basically stops here.


Classification model
This time, you’ll be doing basically the same thing, but with a binary classification model. Create your prediction target (labels) as a Boolean vector by thresholding total benefits < 20,000. This can be done in numpy simply as (for example):
y = total_benefits < 20_000

Count how many labels you have of each class (True or False). In your report, comment on the class balance.
As before, create a Scikit-learn pipeline and pick a classification model. You may copy the same pipeline from the previous task and simply swap out the model; you don’t need to document your processing decisions again.
Once more, pick an appropriate metric and validate your model using cross-validation. Be careful of the class (im)balance!
Again, iterate and try to improve your model based on the results of cross-validation. In your report, make note of what you try and how it impacts the model.
When you’re happy with the results, document your final pipeline in your report. This can just be a copy/paste of your pipeline construction code, formatted neatly as a code block.

title: 3: Categorical Data Representation
text:
Predicting breast cancer recurrance
This is another small dataset, painstakingly collected in the 1980s from real breast cancer patients. Each sample represents an individual with breast cancer, which may or may not have recurred during the time period of the study1. A number of categorical features are recorded for each, along with the target variable (one of no-recurrence-events and recurrence-events).
Each of the following steps is also indicated as TODO items in the starter notebook.

Convert the target into a binary feature, assumed to be named y
Do some basic exploration on the categorical features, paying attention to:

feature cardinality
ordinal vs nominal

There’s also a single continuous value — inspect it using an appropriate visualization or other method
Define appropriate encoders for the categorical features (either OneHotEncoder or OrdinalEncoder). Pay attention to the names of the categories for ordinal encoding! By default they will map to alphabetical order, but that is not the same as numerical order (why?).
Put your encoders into the provided pipeline skeleton, then cross-validate to see how your model behaves. Can you make any changes that improve the performance?







NoteStretch goal



If you want to take things a step further, see if you can interpret the .feature_importances_ attribute of the classifier. You can access this with the last element of the pipeline, i.e.:
importance = pipeline[-1].feature_importances_

title: 3. Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Exploratory data analysis
The goal of EDA is to Understand your data

Ask questions (e.g. do my data fit the linear model assumptions?)
Look for answers (e.g. by making histograms)
Find more questions and return to step 1 (hmm, those are some weird numbers, what do these values represent?)



EDA is not a formal process with a strict set of rules. More than anything, EDA is a state of mind. During the initial phases of EDA you should feel free to investigate every idea that occurs to you. Some of these ideas will pan out, and some will be dead ends. — Hadley Wickham

title: 3. Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Basic things to look at

Data source - File? Database? API?
Structured/unstructured
Assumption 1: relatively small (fits in memory) tabular dataset

Assumption 2: numeric data

Ranges
Summary statistics
Missing values

Next week: categorical data, after reading week unstructured

title: 3. Exploratory Data Analysis
section: Case Study: Data visualization to the rescue
text:
Case Study: Data visualization to the rescue

A 2012 study about honesty reported that “Signing at the beginning makes ethics salient and decreases dishonest self-reports in comparison to signing at the end”
In 2020, the authors published a new paper admitting that their original results could not be replicated, and noticed an anomaly in the summary statistics
The 2020 paper also published the original data, which was downloaded and visualized by a team of anonymous researchers working with Data Colada
This led to the 2012 paper being retracted, a $25M lawsuit, a data-driven defense



Moral of the story is, look at your data!

title: 3. Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Useful starting points

pandas.DataFrame.head: return the first n rows (default 5). Also tail.

Various aggregation statistics

title: 3. Exploratory Data Analysis

Why split your data?



We need to set aside a final test set to evaluate our final model
Humans are great at detecting patterns!
Even looking at test data could influence decisions, causing data leakage


Image source: Spurious Correlations

title: 3. Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
When to split your data

How much EDA should you do before splitting? You might need to know:

Are there any missing values?
Is there a need for stratified sampling?
Do the data have a unique identifier beyond the row label?
As soon as you have a general sense of the:

Data types
Missing features
Distributions, particularly categorical

It’s time to split the data!

title: 3. Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
How to split your data
As usual, it depends on the:

Relationship between number of predictors \(p\) and \(n\)
Nature of the data:

Time series?
Stratification needed?

Intended validation approach

title: 3. Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Validation



We also need validation data
If the dataset is sufficiently large, this can be a separate split
In lab 2 and assignment 1 I asked you to use cross-validation


Image source: Scikit-learn

title: 3. Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Validation

Validation data is used to make decisions about your model, e.g.

Model selection
Tuning hyperparameters
Monitor training progress

However, validation data is not used to directly train a model
Think of it like a test-adjacent set where you can repeatedly try stuff on your training set, then evaluate on validation



Cross-validation is a way of checking your model choice and parameters, but final training should be done on the entire training set

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
text:
Common 1:1 transformations

“Most models work best when each feature (and in regression also the target) is loosely Gaussian distributed” — Introduction to Machine Learning with Python


Scaling: normalization or standardization
Nonlinear transforms: log, square root, polynomial
Fancier methods: Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
section: A brief intro to gradient descent
text:
A brief intro to gradient descent

Many linear models minimize some cost function through gradient descent
The gradient is a vector of partial derivatives \[\nabla f = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \end{bmatrix}\]
for some scalar-valued \(f(\mathbf{x})\)

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
text:
Descending the gradient
For a loss (or cost) function such as \(MSE(\mathrm{\theta}) = \frac{1}{m}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\theta} - \mathbf{y})^T(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\theta} - \mathbf{y})\)

Start with a random \(\mathbf{\theta}\)
Calculate the gradient \(\nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}}\) for the current \(\mathbf{\theta}\)
Update \(\mathbf{\theta}\) as \(\mathbf{\theta} = \mathbf{\theta} - \eta \nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}}\)
Repeat 2-3 until some stopping criterion is met
where \(\eta\) is the learning rate, or the size of step to take in the direction opposite the gradient.

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
text:
Visualizing in 2D

The gradient has \(m + 1\) dimensions, where \(m\) is the number of features
step size \(\eta\) is a scalar parameter





Main takeaway: feature should be more or less on the same scale



Figure 4-7 from Hands-on Machine Learning

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
text:
Approaches to scaling



Standardize: \(x_{scaled} = \dfrac{x - \mu_x}{\sigma_x}\)Normalize: \(x_{scaled} = \dfrac{x - \mathrm{min}(x)}{\mathrm{max}(x) - \mathrm{min}(x)}\)

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
text:
Nonlinear transforms




Common case: count data
Example: Ask 1000 students how often they checked D2L that day
Not a Gaussian distribution!
What about the central limit theorem?

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
text:
Power transforms
A family of functions that map data to a normal distribution.
\[y_i^{(\lambda)} =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{y_i^\lambda-1}{\lambda(\operatorname{GM}(y))^{\lambda -1}} , &\text{if } \lambda \neq 0 \\[12pt]
\operatorname{GM}(y)\ln{y_i} , &\text{if } \lambda = 0
\end{cases}\]
(Or just PowerTransformer)



Image credit: Scikit-learn

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
text:
Transformations in training vs inference

Define functions, e.g.
def standardize(X, mu, sigma):
    return (X - mu) / sigma
Compute scaling parameters on the training data, then stash them somewhere:
mu = X_train.mean()
sigma = X_train.std()
# ... later on, during inference
X = standardize(X, mu, sigma)

What would happen if standardize instead computed values on the fly?

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
text:
Manual approach in the wild
You may run across magic numbers, e.g from the PyTorch tutorials:
import torch
from torchvision import transforms, datasets

data_transform = transforms.Compose([
        transforms.RandomResizedCrop(224),
        transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(),
        transforms.ToTensor(),
        transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406],
                             std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225])
    ])
This really should have a comment! Derived from ImageNet.

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
text:
An alternative solution: Scikit-learn Pipelines

Hard-coding scaling (and other) parameters is okay, provided you can justify the choice and document where they came from
Scikit-learn Pipeline is a convenient alternative
Each step in the pipeline has a fit and transform method

fit computes parameters from the training data
transform applies the transformation
fit_transform does both — only use on training data!

You can call these functions on the whole pipeline to fit or apply all in one go

title: 5: Basic Numeric Transformations
text:
Summary

Numerical data often needs to be transformed to fit model assumptions
Standardizing and normalizing are very common
Nonlinear transformations can also be beneficial
Make sure to only compute parameters based on training data!
